name: Jade Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. What is a normal day on the lines like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At forty-three I still like reaching a fault before the street has gone completely dark. I work for the electricity company: inspect poles, repair damaged power lines, and make the site safe with my crew before anybody climbs. The paperwork at the depot wears on me more than the weather, though I will take rain over a loose connection any day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a new screen will not tighten a loose connector on a pole. If it makes the depot forms quicker, fine, but the job remains ours to finish safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is good for this trade and we have more than six months put aside, but the mortgage still needs the hours. I do not want a supervisor mistaking a tidy software report for a sound repair. A tidy software report cannot tell me whether a connector is loose on a power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts and check the paper work orders against what we find at each pole. In the first year I would put part of each overtime payment into the mortgage, as we already planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a small itch when a manager calls a cheap shortcut an improvement. A mild AI change would not have me searching for another company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the crew see you do differently on an ordinary callout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still ask for the isolation check aloud before the climb. I might mark a wrong pole number on the work order, but the repair sequence stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the mortgage payment change about your answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I have two children still in school, so a missed month of pay is not trivial. We can cover a gap, and paying a little extra when overtime comes keeps that gap manageable.

say: A **screen** can speed depot forms, while the crew still makes the line safe and repairs the fault.
I would **welcome** less clerical work if nobody treats a neat report as proof of a safe repair.
think: Our **strong** savings cushion protects a missed month, yet the mortgage makes steady lineworker hours valuable.
I **distrust** a supervisor who uses a software report to skip the crew’s physical checks.
do: **Keep** my usual shifts and check work orders against each pole before anyone climbs.
**Put** part of each overtime payment toward the mortgage during the first year.
feel: **Steady** about my lineworker job, though wary of management selling a shortcut as safety.
S0.quote: A tidy software report cannot tell me whether a connector is loose on a power line.
fieldNote: Her **apprenticeship** habits remain the measure of a safe repair, even when forms become easier.
**Strong** savings and good wages steady her, while children and a mortgage keep hours relevant.

steps.text: Keep current power line shifts and check each work order at the pole
Pay extra on the mortgage from each overtime payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our crew that dispatch software may route callouts, but a real line still needs hands and eyes. I would also ask our union representative to make sure a faster schedule never means rushed isolation checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could lose planners before anyone takes my tools away. If fewer people handle outages, the pressure may come down to us as tighter time targets, and I dislike that bargain. A power line does not become safe because the dispatch screen says our minutes are up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union safety group to collect examples of schedules that leave too little time for isolation. In the first year I would compare the new dispatch estimates with actual repair times and hand over the differences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy, not frightened for next month’s pay. It gets under my skin when the people setting deadlines have never stood under a live span.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record after a callout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the assigned repair time, the isolation time, and why a second crew was needed. A vague complaint is easy to dismiss; those three times are harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you raise those numbers with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take them to our union safety group, which already meets about near misses. I would want a rule that a crew leader can stop a job without being punished for missing the software estimate.

say: **Dispatch** may improve routing, but physical line repairs still require a crew and proper safety checks.
I would **ask** the union to challenge any schedule that squeezes isolation time.
think: **Automated** planning could remove office planners and send unrealistic targets to field crews.
Our **good** savings do not make a rushed repair acceptable to me or my crew.
do: **Record** dispatch estimates, isolation time, and actual repair time on each new schedule.
**Bring** the timing evidence to the union safety group during the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** about unsafe time targets, while my own field wages still seem reasonably secure.
S1.quote: A power line does not become safe because the dispatch screen says our minutes are up.
fieldNote: Her **public** safety argument also protects the time needed to perform skilled work.
She **expects** planning desks to change earlier than physical repairs and resists rushed field targets.

steps.text: Record dispatch estimates against isolation and repair times
Bring timing records to the union safety group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say that thinking AI arriving by 2028 does not give us permission to send robots onto the lines untested. The crew should have a say in trials before hands-on robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dispatch, fault diagnosis and ordering might change first, but my climbing and repair work lasts longer. Three years is short when a mortgage and two children depend on my higher wages, even with savings behind us. Three years is a short safety trial when my family’s mortgage sits behind every power line shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union to seek paid safety trials and a written process for stopping an unsafe robot job. This year I would hold back on a kitchen renovation and put the monthly amount into a separate emergency account; after 2028 I would watch for lost overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That pace makes me anxious because the rules may lag behind the machines. I can live with a trial, but not with a crew being treated as spare parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a robot trial acceptable to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew leader would need authority to stop it at the first unsafe move, with the same pay for the crew. A demonstration in a yard is not enough for a damaged span in rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much money goes to that emergency account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were setting aside about two hundred a month for the kitchen. I would redirect that new monthly saving into the emergency account for a year and leave the existing savings untouched.

say: I would **demand** crew input and paid safety trials before robots work on power lines.
**Thinking** AI might speed dispatch first; physical line repairs still need safe workers until robots can prove themselves.
think: The **three** years between thinking AI and robots may be too short to protect higher field wages.
Our **mortgage** and children make lost overtime matter despite more than six months of savings.
do: **Ask** the union for paid robot trials and crew authority to stop unsafe work.
**Redirect** two hundred a month from the planned kitchen budget into emergency savings.
feel: **Anxious** about speed and weak safeguards, though a funded cushion leaves room to respond.
S2.quote: Three years is a short safety trial when my family’s mortgage sits behind every power line shift.
fieldNote: The **fast** timetable shifts her from cautious observation to organised safety demands.
She **describes** new monthly saving from a delayed renovation, while keeping existing savings intact.

steps.text: Ask union representatives for paid robot trials and stop-work authority
Pause kitchen renovation and redirect two hundred monthly to emergency savings
Delay planned kitchen purchases for the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues we have a few years before thinking AI reaches full strength in 2031, and another three before capable robots. The company should use that time to test jobs with us, rather than announce a finished plan from headquarters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2034 the children will be older and our mortgage should be smaller if the overtime keeps coming. I could consider a safety inspection role inside the electricity company, but I would need to see its pay before leaving line work. I will not trade my lineworker wage for a safety badge until the inspection salary covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would sit in on the company’s inspection training briefing this year and ask for the pay scale and required certificate. If the terms work, I would apply for paid training in the first year after thinking AI arrives; I would keep field shifts until an offer is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful, with some room to breathe. I still do not want a machine rehearsed in a depot to decide what is safe above a road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you ask at the training briefing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the safety inspection certificate can be earned on paid time and whether its salary would cover our mortgage. If either answer is no, I would stay with the crew and check nearby lineworker vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this mean you have changed your mind about technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am willing to learn an inspection method after it has been tested on real faults. I am not signing up to be the first person trusting an unproven robot over a live line.

say: The **company** has years to involve line crews in safe testing before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would **ask** for real field trials instead of a finished headquarters plan.
think: An **inspection** role could protect income if its pay covers the mortgage and training is paid.
The **children** will be older and the mortgage smaller if overtime remains available.
do: **Attend** the inspection training briefing and request certificate and salary details this year.
**Apply** for paid inspection training after 2031 only if terms cover the mortgage.
**Continue** line shifts until an actual inspection offer exists.
feel: **Watchful** but less pressed, because the longer timetable permits a conditional career move.
S3.quote: I will not trade my lineworker wage for a safety badge until the inspection salary covers our mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **apparent** openness depends on proven field methods and an inspection salary that covers debt.
She **distinguishes** asking about a course now from actually applying after the first AI milestone.

steps.text: Apply for paid inspection training after 2031 if salary covers mortgage
Keep power line shifts until an inspection offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade lets crews bargain over what safe robot work looks like before 2039. I would rather teach the next apprentices how to read a damaged line than pretend the old skills have expired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three in 2036, I may still be working, though the mortgage should be much lower if the payments hold. I can picture doing field inspections and mentoring instead of every climb, but I will not call that retirement. A robot can take the climb, but an apprentice still needs to know when a power line plan is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union training committee this year about a paid mentor slot and its hours. If a slot opens at our electricity company in the first year after 2036, I would apply while keeping line shifts until the pay matches what our household needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier with that much warning. The long view does not make a robot safe, but it gives workers time to set conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take less pay for the mentor role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small drop might be possible once the mortgage has shrunk, but I cannot promise that today. I would check our household budget and the actual offer before taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What skill would you want an apprentice to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make them explain the isolation check aloud at the pole, not only tap a box on a device. A repair on a live street needs a person who knows when the plan is wrong.

say: A **decade** gives line crews time to bargain over safe robot work before hands-on machines arrive around 2039.
I would **pass** physical fault-reading skills to apprentices while standards are still being shaped.
think: A **lower** mortgage could permit mentoring and inspection work, subject to real hours and pay.
I do **not** see a move away from climbing as an automatic retirement decision.
do: **Ask** the union training committee about paid mentor slots and their hours this year.
**Apply** for a company mentor slot after 2036 only if its pay meets household needs.
**Keep** line shifts until a suitable mentor offer is made.
feel: **Steadier** with a decade to shape safe practice, though the machines still need proof.
S4.quote: A robot can take the climb, but an apprentice still needs to know when a power line plan is wrong.
fieldNote: She **imagines** a later role that preserves craft knowledge without calling it retirement.
**Longer** lead time calms her because family debt can shrink before possible job changes.

steps.text: Ask union training committee about paid lineworker mentor slots
Apply for company mentor role after 2036 if pay meets household needs
Keep line shifts until a suitable mentor offer arrives

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a rushed robot rollout could reach the lines before crews can set safe rules. Paid field trials, crew stop-work authority, and enough notice about overtime changes would help us plan around the mortgage. I do not want a speech about progress when a crew is being sent up a pole.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays if a robot damages a line and a worker is told to make it right in the dark. My apprenticeship taught me that responsibility follows the hands doing the repair, but the company also chooses the tools. The people climbing need a voice in that choice.

headlineQuote: I do not want a speech about progress when a crew is being sent up a pole.
portrait: **Jade** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company lineworker whose apprenticeship shapes her insistence on spoken isolation checks and real field evidence.
**Higher** wages and over six months of savings buffer her household, while two school-age children and a mortgage make reliable shifts matter.
She **accepts** minor paperwork gains but distrusts schedules or robots that turn a neat screen into an excuse to rush physical repairs.
**Union** safety work grows urgent by 2028; with more time, she considers paid inspection or mentoring on acceptable terms.
biggestWorry: **Fast** AGI by 2028 could bring hands-on robots to line work around 2031 before crews have safe rules.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** field trials, crew stop-work authority, and clear notice about overtime changes would let her plan around the mortgage.
